summary.text: Writing each factorial as its lower factorial times a power of \(p\) and a product of \(p\)-free terms reduces the comparison at \(L p\) and \(L\), with \(p^t\mid L\), to residue products in blocks of length \(q=p^{t+1}\). Pairing \(u\) with \(q-u\) and using \(\sum_{u\in(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times}u^{-2}=0\) gives invariance of each full block modulo \(q^3\); the even case then cancels directly, while the odd case uses the half-integer Gamma duplication formula and a Morley-type identity relating the centered half-block, the full unit block, and the required power of \(2\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(m)=\frac{\Gamma(9m+1)\Gamma(2m+1)\Gamma(3m/2+1)}
 {\Gamma(9m/2+1)\Gamma(4m+1)\Gamma(3m+1)\Gamma(m+1)}.
\]
The accepted statement assumes the separate integrality assertion that every real number \(a(m)\) is an integer. Under that hypothesis, denote by \(A_m\in\mathbb Z\) the unique integer whose image in \(\mathbb R\) is \(a(m)\). We prove that for every prime \(p\geq5\), every \(n>0\), and every \(r>0\),
\[
 A_{np^r}\equiv A_{np^{r-1}}\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]

Throughout the proof, products and sums modulo an integer are taken in the corresponding residue ring. Every integer prime to \(p\) is a unit modulo every power of \(p\), so such factors may be cancelled.

## 1. Reduced-residue products

For a prime \(p\), define
\[
 W_p(x)=\prod_{\substack{1\leq j\leq x\\p\nmid j}}j.
\]
Fix for the moment an integer \(t\geq0\), and put
\[
 q=p^{t+1},\qquad
 I=\{u:1\leq u<q,\ p\nmid u\}.
\]
Thus \(I\) is a complete set of units modulo \(q\).

We first establish the inverse-square identity
\[
 \sum_{u\in I}u^{-2}=0\pmod q. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, if \(U=(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times\), multiplication by \(2\) permutes \(U\). Hence, writing \(S=\sum_{u\in U}u^2\),
\[
 S=\sum_{u\in U}(2u)^2=4S.
\]
Thus \(3S=0\). Since \(p\geq5\), both \(2\) and \(3\) are units modulo \(q\), so \(S=0\). Inversion also permutes \(U\), and consequently
\[
 \sum_{u\in U}u^{-2}=\sum_{u\in U}u^2=0,
\]
which is (1).

We need a lifted form of Wilson's product argument. The following version will also be used later.

**Lifted product lemma.** Let \(q\geq5\), and let \(S\) be a finite set of integers such that:

1. every \(u\in S\) is a unit modulo \(q\);
2. for some positive integer \(d\), the reflection \(u\mapsto dq-u\) permutes \(S\);
3. \(u\leq dq\) for every \(u\in S\);
4. \(\sum_{u\in S}u^{-2}=0\pmod q\).

Then, for every \(N\geq0\),
\[
 \prod_{u\in S}(Nq+u)\equiv\prod_{u\in S}u\pmod {q^3}. \tag{2}
\]

To prove this, work in \(R=\mathbb Z/q^3\mathbb Z\), write \(Q\) for the class of \(q\), and set
\[
 B_N=\prod_{u\in S}(Nq+u),\qquad B_0=\prod_{u\in S}u.
\]
Since reflection permutes \(S\),
\[
 B_N^2=\prod_{u\in S}(Nq+u)(Nq+dq-u).
\]
For each \(u\), direct expansion gives
\[
 (Nq+u)(Nq+dq-u)=u(dq-u)+N(N+d)q^2.
\]
Put \(e=N(N+d)Q^2\). Since \(Q^3=0\) in \(R\), one has \(e^2=0\). Therefore the elementary first-order product expansion
\[
 \prod_{u\in S}(x_u+e)
 =\prod_{u\in S}x_u+e\sum_{u\in S}\prod_{v\in S\setminus\{u\}}x_v \tag{3}
\]
holds: every term involving two or more copies of \(e\) vanishes.

Take \(x_u=u(dq-u)\). Reflection shows
\[
 \prod_{u\in S}x_u
 =\left(\prod_{u\in S}u\right)
  \left(\prod_{u\in S}(dq-u)\right)=B_0^2.
\]
It remains to show that the correction term in (3) vanishes. Modulo \(q\),
\[
 x_u=u(dq-u)\equiv-u^2,
\]
and hence
\[
 x_u^{-1}\equiv-u^{-2}\pmod q.
\]
Thus
\[
 \sum_{u\in S}\prod_{v\ne u}x_v
 =\left(\prod_{v\in S}x_v\right)\sum_{u\in S}x_u^{-1}
 \equiv-\left(\prod_{v\in S}x_v\right)\sum_{u\in S}u^{-2}
 \equiv0\pmod q.
\]
The correction is this sum multiplied by \(e\), which contains \(q^2\), so it is zero modulo \(q^3\). We have proved \(B_N^2=B_0^2\) in \(R\).

Finally, \(B_N+B_0\) is a unit modulo \(q^3\). Indeed, modulo \(q\),
\[
 B_N+B_0\equiv 2B_0,
\]
and both \(2\) and \(B_0\) are units. Hence from
\[
 (B_N-B_0)(B_N+B_0)=B_N^2-B_0^2=0
\]
we may cancel \(B_N+B_0\), obtaining \(B_N=B_0\). This proves (2).

Apply the lemma with \(d=1\) and \(S=I\). The reflection \(u\mapsto q-u\) preserves \(I\), and (1) supplies the inverse-square condition. Therefore
\[
 \prod_{u\in I}(Nq+u)\equiv \prod_{u\in I}u\pmod {q^3}. \tag{4}
\]
Let
\[
 B=\prod_{u\in I}u\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/q^3\mathbb Z.
\]
Partitioning \([1,sq]\) into \(s\) consecutive blocks of length \(q\), and using (4) on each block, gives
\[
 W_p(sq)\equiv B^s\pmod {q^3}. \tag{5}
\]
Notice that \(B\) is a unit.

We shall repeatedly use the factorial decomposition
\[
 N!=p^{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}\lfloor N/p\rfloor!\,W_p(N). \tag{6}
\]
This follows by splitting the factors in \(N!\) into those divisible by \(p\) and those not divisible by \(p\). The divisible factors are precisely
\(p,2p,\ldots,\lfloor N/p\rfloor p\), whose product is the first two factors on the right of (6). In particular,
\[
 (Mp)!=p^M M!W_p(Mp). \tag{7}
\]

## 2. Even indices

For an even index \(m=2k\), all gamma arguments are integers, and \(\Gamma(s+1)=s!\) gives
\[
 A_{2k}=
 \frac{(18k)!(4k)!(3k)!}{(9k)!(8k)!(6k)!(2k)!}. \tag{8}
\]
Equivalently, as an identity of integers,
\[
 A_{2k}(9k)!(8k)!(6k)!(2k)!=(18k)!(4k)!(3k)!. \tag{9}
\]

Suppose \(p^t\mid k\), say \(k=p^t s\). Apply (7) to every factorial in (9) with \(k\) replaced by \(kp\). The total exponent of \(p\) on the denominator side is
\((9+8+6+2)k=25k\), and that on the numerator side is
\((18+4+3)k=25k\). Comparing the identities (9) at \(k\) and at \(kp\), and cancelling the common nonzero integer factorial and \(p\)-power factors, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&A_{2kp}W_p(9kp)W_p(8kp)W_p(6kp)W_p(2kp)\\
&\qquad=A_{2k}W_p(18kp)W_p(4kp)W_p(3kp). \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(cpk=(cs)q\), formula (5) says
\[
 W_p(cpk)\equiv B^{cs}\pmod {q^3}. \tag{11}
\]
The total exponent of \(B\) on either side of (10) is \(25s\). It is a unit, so cancellation yields
\[
 A_{2kp}\equiv A_{2k}\pmod {q^3}.
\]
Since \(q^3=p^{3+3t}\), we have proved
\[
 p^{3+3t}\mid A_{2kp}-A_{2k}\qquad(p^t\mid k). \tag{12}
\]

## 3. Half-block products and a generalized Morley congruence

The odd-index case requires a second product congruence. Since \(q\) is odd, define
\[
 H=\{u:1\leq u\leq(q-1)/2,\ p\nmid u\},
\]
\[
 C=\{u:(q+1)/2\leq u<q,\ p\nmid u\},
\]
and
\[
 S_2=\{u:(q+1)/2\leq u\leq(3q-1)/2,\ p\nmid u\}.
\]
Thus \(I=H\sqcup C\), and reflection \(u\mapsto q-u\) gives a bijection from \(H\) to \(C\). Since inverse squares are unchanged by sign, the sums over \(H\) and \(C\) are equal. Their sum is zero by (1); as \(2\) is a unit modulo \(q\),
\[
 \sum_{u\in H}u^{-2}=0\pmod q. \tag{13}
\]
Also
\[
 S_2=C\sqcup(q+H).
\]
Consequently its inverse-square sum is the sum over \(C\) plus that over \(H\), hence is zero modulo \(q\). The set \(S_2\) is preserved by reflection \(u\mapsto2q-u\). The lifted product lemma, now with \(d=2\), gives
\[
 \prod_{u\in S_2}(Nq+u)\equiv\prod_{u\in S_2}u\pmod {q^3}. \tag{14}
\]
Put
\[
 \mathcal H=\prod_{u\in H}u,
 \qquad G=\prod_{u\in S_2}u
\]
in \(\mathbb Z/q^3\mathbb Z\). Splitting an interval ending halfway through a block into its initial half-block and subsequent full shifted blocks, and using (14), gives
\[
 W_p\left(\frac{q-1}{2}+Nq\right)
 \equiv \mathcal H G^N\pmod {q^3}. \tag{15}
\]
Here \(q/2\) in integer notation means \((q-1)/2\).

We next prove the generalized Morley identity
\[
 2^{2|I|}G=B\pmod {q^3}, \tag{16}
\]
where
\[
 |I|=p^t(p-1). \tag{17}
\]
The count (17) follows because among \(1,\ldots,q-1\), exactly \(p^t-1\) numbers are divisible by \(p\); thus
\((q-1)-(p^t-1)=q-p^t=p^t(p-1)\) remain.

For the proof of (16), continue to work modulo \(q^3\), and abbreviate
\[
 \rho=\prod_{w\in H}(1+q/w),\qquad
 \tau=\prod_{w\in H}(1+q/(2w)),
\]
\[
 \Pi=\prod_{u\in C}(1+q/(2u-q)).
\]
All displayed denominators are units. We prove four elementary relations.

First,
\[
 G=B\rho. \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, \(S_2=C\sqcup(q+H)\), so
\[
 G=\left(\prod_{u\in C}u\right)
   \left(\prod_{w\in H}(q+w)\right)
 =\left(\prod_{u\in C}u\right)
   \left(\prod_{w\in H}w\right)\rho=B\rho.
\]

Second,
\[
 \tau\Pi=1. \tag{19}
\]
The doubling map partitions the complete reduced residues \(I\) as
\[
 I=\{2w:w\in H\}\sqcup\{2u-q:u\in C\}.
\]
Applying (4) with \(N=1\), factoring \(u+q=u(1+q/u)\), and cancelling \(B\), gives
\[
 \prod_{v\in I}(1+q/v)=1.
\]
Using the displayed doubling partition turns this exactly into (19).

Third,
\[
 2^{|I|}=\Pi. \tag{20}
\]
On the one hand,
\[
 \prod_{v\in I}2v=2^{|I|}B.
\]
On the other hand, split \(I=H\sqcup C\). The doubled residues are \(2w\) for \(w\in H\), while for \(u\in C\),
\[
 2u=(2u-q)\left(1+\frac q{2u-q}\right).
\]
The products of the base factors \(2w\) and \(2u-q\) together equal \(B\), because those factors form the doubling partition of \(I\). Hence
\[
 \prod_{v\in I}2v=B\Pi.
\]
Cancel \(B\) to obtain (20).

Fourth,
\[
 \rho=\tau^2. \tag{21}
\]
Let \(\iota=2^{-1}\) modulo \(q^3\). For each \(w\in H\),
\[
 \left(1+\frac q{2w}\right)^2
 =1+\frac qw+q^2\iota^2w^{-2}.
\]
When these identities are multiplied over \(H\), every product containing two of the final \(q^2\)-terms vanishes modulo \(q^3\). The total first-order correction is
\[
 q^2\iota^2\sum_{w\in H}w^{-2}
 \prod_{v\in H\setminus\{w\}}(1+q/v).
\]
Modulo the extra factor \(q^2\), each remaining product may be replaced by \(1\). Thus this correction equals
\(q^2\iota^2\sum_{w\in H}w^{-2}\), which vanishes by (13). What remains is precisely \(\rho\), proving (21).

Now (18)--(21) imply
\[
 2^{2|I|}G
 =B\,2^{2|I|}\rho
 =B\,\Pi^2\tau^2
 =B(\Pi\tau)^2=B,
\]
which is (16).

## 4. Odd indices

For \(m=2j+1\), use the half-integer gamma formula
\[
 \Gamma\left(M+\frac32\right)
 =\frac{(2M+1)!\sqrt\pi}{2^{2M+1}M!}.
\]
Substitution in the definition of \(a(m)\) cancels the two occurrences of \(\sqrt\pi\) and gives
\[
 A_{2j+1}
 =\frac{2^{12j+6}(4j+2)!(9j+4)!}
 {(3j+1)!(8j+4)!(2j+1)!}. \tag{22}
\]
Thus
\[
 A_{2j+1}(3j+1)!(8j+4)!(2j+1)!
 =2^{12j+6}(4j+2)!(9j+4)!. \tag{23}
\]

We first compare (23) at two indices related by multiplication by \(p\). Put
\[
 m_0=\frac{p-1}{2},\qquad J=jp+m_0.
\]
Then
\[
 2J+1=(2j+1)p,
\]
and direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
8J+4&=(8j+4)p,&4J+2&=(4j+2)p,\\
3J+1&=p(3j+1)+m_0,&9J+4&=p(9j+4)+m_0.
\end{aligned} \tag{24}
\]
Since \(0\leq m_0<p\), the last two numbers have quotients \(3j+1\) and \(9j+4\), respectively, upon division by \(p\). Apply (6) to all five factorials in (23) at \(J\), and compare with (23) at \(j\). The total extracted \(p\)-power is \(p^{13j+6}\) on each side, and hence cancels. Also
\[
 12J+6=6(2j+1)(p-1)+(12j+6).
\]
After cancelling the remaining common factorial products via (23) at \(j\), one obtains the exact integer identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
&A_{(2j+1)p}W_p(3J+1)W_p((8j+4)p)W_p((2j+1)p)\\
&\quad=2^{6(2j+1)(p-1)}A_{2j+1}
 W_p((4j+2)p)W_p(9J+4). \tag{25}
\end{aligned}
\]

Now suppose
\[
 p^t\mid 2j+1,
 \qquad 2j+1=p^t s.
\]
Both \(p^t\) and \(2j+1\) are odd, so \(s\) is odd. Since \(q=p^{t+1}\),
\[
 (2j+1)p=sq,
\]
and therefore
\[
 2J+1=sq. \tag{26}
\]
Formula (5) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_p((2j+1)p)&\equiv B^s,\\
W_p((8j+4)p)&\equiv B^{4s},\\
W_p((4j+2)p)&\equiv B^{2s}.
\end{aligned} \tag{27}
\]
Because \(s,q,3s,9s\) are odd, elementary division by \(2\), using (26), gives
\[
 3J+1=\frac{q-1}{2}+\frac{3s-1}{2}q,
\qquad
 9J+4=\frac{q-1}{2}+\frac{9s-1}{2}q. \tag{28}
\]
Hence (15) gives
\[
 W_p(3J+1)\equiv\mathcal H G^{(3s-1)/2},
\quad
 W_p(9J+4)\equiv\mathcal H G^{(9s-1)/2}. \tag{29}
\]

The exponent of \(2\) in (25) can be expressed using (17):
\[
 6(2j+1)(p-1)=6p^ts(p-1)=2|I|\,(3s). \tag{30}
\]
Raising the Morley congruence (16) to the \(3s\)-th power and using (30), we obtain
\[
 2^{6(2j+1)(p-1)}G^{3s}=B^{3s}\pmod {q^3}. \tag{31}
\]
Also
\[
 \frac{9s-1}{2}=\frac{3s-1}{2}+3s. \tag{32}
\]

Substitute (27) and (29) into (25), and use (32). Its left-hand auxiliary product becomes
\[
 \mathcal H G^{(3s-1)/2}B^{5s},
\]
while on the right the extra factors are transformed, by (31), into exactly the same product. More explicitly, the right side contains
\[
 2^{6(2j+1)(p-1)}B^{2s}\mathcal H
 G^{(3s-1)/2}G^{3s}
 =\mathcal H G^{(3s-1)/2}B^{5s}.
\]
Thus (25) reduces modulo \(q^3\) to
\[
 A_{(2j+1)p}\,\mathcal H G^{(3s-1)/2}B^{5s}
 \equiv A_{2j+1}\,\mathcal H G^{(3s-1)/2}B^{5s}.
\]
Every factor in \(\mathcal H\), \(G\), and \(B\) is prime to \(p\); hence the common product is a unit modulo \(q^3\). Cancelling it gives
\[
 A_{(2j+1)p}\equiv A_{2j+1}\pmod {q^3}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 p^{3+3t}\mid A_{(2j+1)p}-A_{2j+1}
 \qquad\text{whenever }p^t\mid2j+1. \tag{33}
\]

## 5. The one-step congruence and conclusion

Let \(L>0\) and suppose \(p^t\mid L\). We claim
\[
 p^{3+3t}\mid A_{Lp}-A_L. \tag{34}
\]
If \(L\) is odd, write \(L=2j+1\); then (34) is exactly (33). If \(L\) is even, write \(L=2k\). Since \(p\) is odd, \(p^t\) is coprime to \(2\). The divisibility \(p^t\mid2k\) therefore implies \(p^t\mid k\), and (34) follows from (12). This exhausts the two parity cases.

Finally take
\[
 L=np^{r-1},\qquad t=r-1.
\]
Because \(n,r>0\), \(L>0\), and plainly \(p^{r-1}\mid L\). Also
\[
 Lp=np^r,
 \qquad 3+3(r-1)=3r.
\]
Applying (34) yields
\[
 p^{3r}\mid A_{np^r}-A_{np^{r-1}},
\]
or equivalently
\[
 \boxed{A_{np^r}\equiv A_{np^{r-1}}\pmod {p^{3r}}}.
\]
This is the desired supercongruence for the integer values of the stated gamma-factorial ratio.
